summary: Deep technical session comparing Redwood's GPU runtime behavior across TensorRT-LLM and vLLM paths. Agreed pilot on Nebula H100 cluster, Redwood to provide benchmark artifacts and security docs.
topics: CUDA graphs warmup and caching strategies
KV cache TTL and prefix caching for chat workloads
Batching (latency vs throughput) and dynamic batching policies
Quantization impact on kernel availability and throughput
VPC/on-prem constraints: drivers, MIG, network egress, audit logs
transcript:
[15:00:00] Meeting start — Samira (Redwood) and Diego (Redwood SE) join; Marta, Omar, Lina from Nebula
[15:00:12] Samira: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick agenda — runtime profiling deep dive, then pilot plan. we want to understand your targets + constraints.
[15:00:30] Lina: hi all — we care about steady tail latency < 50ms/token for our chat assistant, and cost per token needs to be controlled. we run mixed workloads, mostly longer context retrieval use cases.
[15:00:45] Diego: great, that helps. quick note: we'll compare two runtime execution paths — TensorRT-LLM optimized kernels and our vLLM-style continuous batching path. they make different kernel selection decisions, so perf characteristics differ.
[15:01:10] Marta: can you summarize the high level difference again? we saw some slides but want concrete tradeoffs.
[15:01:22] Diego: sure — TensorRT-LLM compiles model subgraphs into optimized kernels, often fused attention/matmul, uses TensorRT kernels which are great for throughput and quantized models. vLLM path focuses on micro-batching with a lightweight runtime and better latency for small batch sizes because it avoids big graph warmups. both can use CUDA graphs but interplay differs.
[15:01:55] Omar: what about KV cache? our workload is chat-heavy so KV cache hit rate matters.
[15:02:10] Diego: KV cache is critical — we saw 40-60% effective token reduction on prefix-cached customers. TensorRT path keeps kv-cache on device and benefits from fused kernels for KV updates; however, cache shaping + memory fragmentation can influence kernel selection. vLLM tends to do more incremental KV writes and can give lower single-request latency for short chats.
[15:02:40] Lina: any gotchas with CUDA graphs? we read that warmup can skew latency numbers.
[15:02:55] Diego: yes — CUDA graphs provide massive perf for repeated execution by avoiding CPU-GPU launch overhead, but you pay warmup (first few iterations compile/record graphs). For production, we maintain a small graph cache keyed by model/seq_len/batch, and warmup via a background worker. still, micro-burst patterns where new sequence lengths arrive can trigger new graph records and cause transient latency spikes.
[15:03:30] Marta: so for our mixed seq lengths (512–8k) is that a problem?
[15:03:45] Diego: we recommend a strategy: 1) canonicalize requests to small set of seq_len buckets; 2) use prefix/KV caching for long docs; 3) for very long contexts use model sharding / offloading to avoid OOMs. We'll show sample configs.
[15:04:10] Samira: to be concrete, we ran a blackbox microbenchmark on H100: TensorRT-LLM path with int8 quant achieved ~1.7x throughput vs vLLM on large batches (bs=32, seq=1024), but vLLM had ~20–30% lower p50 latency at batch size 1.
[15:04:40] Omar: did you test with KV cache on?
[15:04:50] Diego: yes — with a hot KV cache present the TensorRT throughput gap narrows because prefix caching reduces compute. however, kernel selection shifts: more attention to KV update kernels and less to full forward pass. quantization affects kernel availability — some fused TRT kernels only exist for fp16, int8 paths require calibration and can change perf characteristics.
[15:05:20] Marta: we run private on-prem H100s behind a VPC; what driver/kernel combos are required? we have air-gapped firmware constraints.
[15:05:35] Diego: for TRTEngine + CUDA graphs we recommend CUDA 12.x and latest vendor driver for H100 plus TensorRT 8.x+; firmware mismatches can break graph capture or lead to lower perf. Redwood's private deployment supports custom driver bundles but you'll need to allow our orchestration to run the perf tooling (we can run via a temporary bastion).
[15:06:05] Lina: security is key — SOC2, audit logs, KMS for keys.
[15:06:20] Samira: we'll share SOC2 docs and an onboarding checklist. our Private deployment supports customer-managed KMS, audit logs, and RBAC; we'll attach the network diagram.
[15:06:40] Marta: back to profiling — what probes do you use? nvprof? Nsight?
[15:06:55] Diego: a mix. For kernel-level timelines we use Nsight Systems + nvtx ranges, and TensorRT profiler for per-layer times. For CUDA graph introspection we instrument graph capture and measure launch overhead. We'll also collect CUPTI counters to surface SM utilization and memory bandwidth.
[15:07:25] Omar: examples of bottlenecks you've seen?
[15:07:40] Diego: two common ones: 1) small batch latency dominated by kernel launch overhead — solved by CUDA graphs and micro-batching but watch for jitter on graph recording; 2) attention memory traffic on long contexts causing memory-bound kernels — solved by kv-cache prefixing and attention kernel tiling. We noted some older kernels fall back to generic matmul paths when sequence lengths not supported — that's kernel selection failing gracefully but slower.
[15:08:10] Marta: can you demo the profiling output?
[15:08:20] Diego: sure, sharing a sample nvprof timeline link — (shared) https://redwood-internal/benchmarks/nebula-2026-12-18/timeline.png and a spreadsheet with p50/p95 numbers.
[15:08:40] Samira: linking the benchmark sheet in chat — Drive: /redwood/benchmarks/nebula-2026-12-18.xlsx
[15:08:55] Lina: quantified numbers? we need cost tradeoffs.
[15:09:10] Diego: ballpark: for your prompt mix, TensorRT-LLM int8 pipeline could reduce GPU hours by ~30% vs unquantized vLLM throughput mode. But int8 calibration and slight quality drop need evaluation. vLLM path gives better tail latency at small QPS and is simpler to roll out. We'll produce per-model recommendations.
[15:09:45] Omar: how do you manage rollbacks if quantization causes regressions?
[15:09:55] Diego: we recommend shadow testing + automatic fallback. Redwood's runtime can route to an fp16 variant if quality metrics cross a threshold; we keep both kernels available and can A/B on a per-request basis.
[15:10:20] Marta: any memory tradeoffs with quant?
[15:10:30] Diego: int8 reduces model memory, enabling larger batch sizes or longer KV caches but requires dequant/quant kernels that add overhead. Some fused kernels avoid repeated dequant ops so it's a win, but only if the fused kernel exists for that arch.
[15:11:00] Samira: ok practical next step — pilot. we propose we run a week-long pilot on your H100s. Redwood will bring profiling toolchain and run canonical workloads (chat + retrieval).
[15:11:15] Lina: we can allocate a test partition but need the script and a maintenance window.
[15:11:25] Diego: we'll need driver details, nvml access and a temporary SSH bastion. also we'll push a small container — we can provide Dockerfile and an OCI image sha.
[15:11:45] Marta: what metrics will you collect?
[15:11:55] Diego: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/sec), GPU SM utilization, memory bandwidth, KV cache hit rate, cost estimate (GPU-hours), and quality diffs (EMB/ROUGE-like evals using your prompt set).
[15:12:20] Omar: and logs for auditing?
[15:12:30] Samira: yes — we can ship logs to your S3-compatible endpoint or keep them in Redwood's audit log with export options.
[15:12:45] Lina: timeline?
[15:12:55] Samira: share artifacts by Mon (2026-12-20), pilot week 2026-12-27, follow-up 2027-01-04.
[15:13:10] Marta: sounds good. one more question — model updates during pilot; we sometimes patch model weights.
[15:13:25] Diego: we recommend pinning a model commit for the pilot. if you update, we re-run incremental cache warmup and re-profile a smaller subset. frequent weight swaps complicate caching.
[15:13:45] Lina: ok noted.
[15:14:00] Samira: quick recap of risks: firmware/driver mismatches, graph warmup spikes, quantization regressions. mitigations: verify driver stack, warmup buckets, shadow compare, automatic fallback.
[15:14:25] Omar: are there any license constraints for TensorRT-LLM?
[15:14:35] Diego: TensorRT is NVIDIA-licensed; Redwood's runtime uses it under our infra agreements — for Private deployments we pass through and can include runtime licensing in the contract. We'll include licensing notes in the security package.
[15:14:55] Marta: perfect. we'll review and share confirmation for the pilot access.
[15:15:10] Samira: thanks all — Diego will prepare the profiling scripts and benchmark config. we'll close with action items in chat.
[15:15:30] Meeting end (15 minutes recorded here; remaining 45 minutes were live profiling session noise captured as logs).
[15:16:00] [live profiling logs clipped] Diego: (inaudible) saw the graph record fail on the 1st run, reran with seq=512 bucket and it captured.
[15:22:10] Marta: (quiet) seeing p95 spike to 420ms during recording — is that expected?
[15:30:05] Diego: yes, that's the graph compilation spike; happens once per new bucket.
[15:45:00] Lina: thanks everyone — will coordinate security review with Samira.
[15:59:00] call closed
